newsitem.title: SENEGAL: Voting in Senegal poll extended to midnight.
newsitem.headline: Voting in Senegal poll extended to midnight.

text.p: Authorities in Senegal on Sunday extended voting in chaotic local elections to midnight after opposition leaders charged that delays and poor organisation were a ploy to rig the government-run polls.
Many polling stations in the capital Dakar had still not opened by the official close of polls at 6 p.m. (1800 GMT).
Dakar's governor Mahame Diallo said in a statement on state radio that polls would stay open until midnight to allow as many people as possible to cast their ballots.
He spoke for the capital but officials of the interior ministry, which organised the local, ward and regional elections, said governors of each region would decide whether to extend balloting.

Correspondents for private radio stations reported scenes of confusion in the interior similar to that in Dakar, where voters complained of a shortage of everything from voter lists and cards to polling officials.

"As a Senegalese I'm ashamed that at the dawn of the 21st century, we are unable to organise elections," said chief opposition leader Abdoulaye Wade, who is also a minister in President Abdou Diouf's Socialist Party-led government.
"It is deliberate so that under the cover of darkness the Socialist Party will rig the ballots," he said.

The elections in Dakar are seen as a test of popularity between Wade and Diouf, whose Socialist Party is trying to recapture the urban vote it lost to the opposition in presidential and parliamentary polls in 1993.
Wade hopes to emerge as mayor of Dakar.
Other opposition leaders called for suspension of the vote.
"We cannot continue like this. The elections in Dakar have to be postponed and rerun in about two weeks," said lower education minister Mamadou Ndoye, leader of the Democratic League party.
Voting started slowly with people complaining of the same logistics woes that have marred recent ballots in West Africa.
Even the capital's Dakar-Plateau main polling station where Diouf was registered had not received voter cards more than an hour after polls opened at 8 a.m. (0800 GMT).
"If things are this way at this main polling station where the president is supposed to vote, imagine what is happening elsewhere," one voter said.
Just over three million voters were casting their ballots, with 14 parties competing for for 826 regional council seats, 421 municipal council seats, 3,559 district seats and 15,386 rural seats.
